k: Letting teams automate their own work, without waiting for developers

A B2B platform’s customers depended on developers and an internal solutions team for every automated process. I led the design of a low-code workflow builder from scratch, so admins could build, test and run their own workflows. It’s now live with customers.
Every new workflow needed developers or the solutions team, so automation was slow, expensive and out of customers’ hands.
Led the design of the builder from scratch: a free-form canvas, a grouped node library, step-by-step testing, and a run history that shows exactly where a run failed.
Live with customers. Teams now build workflows without the tech or solutions team, set up new workflows faster, and raise fewer support requests.

k.i: Cover: a workflow on the canvas

k: Automation that customers couldn’t do themselves
The platform helps companies run processes like customer onboarding, vendor onboarding and approvals. But every new automated workflow had to be built by developers or the internal solutions team.

That made automation slow to set up, costly to change, and dependent on people outside the customer’s own team. The goal: let customers build their own workflows, with no dependency on the tech or solutions teams.
A workflow builder serves two groups at once, and both had to work well.
They set up processes for their company: forms, conditions, approvals and integrations. They know the business, not necessarily the technology.
They fill in forms and approve steps inside a running workflow, often without knowing a workflow exists at all.
Learning how workflows really get built

I combined four sources: interviews with admins and customers, watching our solutions team build real workflows, feedback from sales, support and demos, and a close study of n8n, Zapier and Microsoft Power Automate.
They describe a process as “collect details, verify, get approval”, not as nodes, triggers and requests.
A node library grouped by what each step does, with a short description of each.
Choosing and configuring nodes was hard
Even experienced builders weren’t always sure which node fit, or how to set it up correctly.
A dedicated page for each node, with its settings on one side and live input and output on the other.
People couldn’t see whether a step worked until the whole workflow ran for real.
“Execute step”: test any single step and see its real output before publishing.
When a run failed, it took time to find which step broke and why.
A run history that shows each run’s path on the canvas and the step that failed.
What I learned from other tools
What we took, and where we differed
A free-form node canvas with powerful logic, and the data in and out of each step
Took: the free-form canvas and visible input and output. Differed: grouped nodes by purpose and added built-in business steps like forms and approvals
Very approachable, with simple step-by-step automations
Took: clear, short descriptions for every step. Differed: chose a canvas so branching processes stay readable
Took: approvals and role-based steps as first-class nodes. Differed: kept the whole process on one visual canvas
03  My role and how I led
Leading the design from a blank page
I was the lead designer, working with other designers, a product manager and engineering. I owned the overall experience, from the canvas and node library to testing and run history.
I divided the work across designers and guided them, so every part of the builder followed the same patterns.
I ran design reviews to check each flow against real use cases and what could be built.
I created the builder’s components, like nodes, connectors and panels, in the design system, so the canvas stayed consistent.
Working with engineers on the canvas
I worked closely with engineers on what the canvas could do: connecting, branching, zooming and showing runs.
A builder for business admins that can still run real enterprise processes forces choices. Each one had a cost, and I chose knowingly.
Real processes branch: approved or rejected, verified or not. The structure of the builder decides whether people can see the whole process at once.
A guided, step-by-step list; a canvas with guided templates; a free-form canvas.
A free-form canvas, where people add steps with “+”, branch with conditions, and see the whole process as one flowchart.
Less hand-holding for first-time admins, in exchange for processes that stay readable as they grow.

k.i: A node’s page: parameters, input and output, Execute step

k: A full page for each step
Steps like forms, HTTP requests and code have many settings. Cramming them into a small panel would hide the most important thing: what data goes in and what comes out.
A side panel on the canvas; a pop-up; a dedicated page per step.
A dedicated page for every node: settings on the left, live input and output on the right, and “Execute step” to test it there and then.
People leave the canvas to configure a step, but they can see and test exactly what it does.
Node names had to work for admins, for the solutions team and for engineers integrating other systems.
Business-friendly names; technical names; technical names with plain descriptions.
Standard names like HTTP, Webhook, If and Loop, matching how other tools and integrators talk, grouped by purpose with a short description in the library.
Familiar to technical users and partners, but harder for business admins, a gap I came back to later.

k.i: The node library, grouped by purpose
Advanced nodes alongside forms and approvals

k: Enterprise processes need real logic: loops, code and calls to other systems. Hiding them would force customers back to developers, the very problem we set out to solve.
Hide advanced nodes; put them behind an “advanced” mode; keep them available to everyone.
Loops, code and HTTP stay available to everyone, so no workflow hits a ceiling that sends people back to the tech team.
The builder leans a little technical. That was a conscious choice, and it shaped what came next.
From a blank canvas to a running process
Four moments carry the whole experience: starting, building, testing and fixing.
An empty canvas asks one thing: how should this workflow start? A form, a condition, AI or a webhook.
“+” opens the library: steps grouped by what they do, with search and a short description.
Execute any step on its own and see its real output before the workflow goes live.
Every run is listed with its status; open one to see its path on the canvas and retry.
The builder is live with customers. What we observed after launch:
Admins now create workflows themselves, without waiting for the tech or solutions team.
New workflows go from idea to running faster, because building no longer passes through another team.
Testing steps before publishing and seeing exactly where a run failed meant fewer questions to support.
These are observed outcomes; the team didn’t measure them with numbers.
Closing the gap I chose to leave
Leaning technical gave customers power, but admins who think in business steps still found it hard to pick the right node. Internal users and support saw the same pattern.
An AI assistant for the builder
Admins describe a workflow in plain words, and the assistant drafts it with the right nodes, then asks before creating it. This became my next project.
Keep the standard names, but lead with what each step does, like “Call another system (HTTP)”.
Ready-made workflows for common processes like onboarding and approvals, so admins start from something that works.
See the AI assistant case study
Every builder sits somewhere between simple and powerful. Choosing where, on purpose, and being honest about what that costs, matters more than trying to be both at once.
Test the node names and library with business admins earlier. The gap between how they think and how the builder speaks showed up after launch, and could have been found sooner.
